summary: git reset moves a branch back to an older commit and drops the newer ones. git revert keeps history and adds a new commit that undoes an old one.
notes: Use reset only on commits you have not pushed. Use revert on commits other people already have.
reset --hard also resets your files. reset --soft keeps the changes staged, and plain reset keeps them unstaged.
git revert can undo any commit, not only the newest. Name it with its hash.
pitfall: git reset --hard deletes uncommitted changes with no undo. Run git status first, and commit or stash anything you want to keep.
setup_note: Starts with four commits on main. The first three were already pushed and the team has them. The newest commit, "Add debug print", was never pushed.
setup:
cat > gradebook.py <<'EOF'
scores = [88, 92, 79, 95]
average = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print("Average:", average)
EOF
git add -A && git commit -q -m "Add gradebook script"

cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# Gradebook
Quiz scores for Period 3.
EOF
git add -A && git commit -q -m "Drop the lowest score"
git add -A && git commit -q -m "Add debug print"
